Sent a screenshot with one sentence: the city's floor isn't there. And then the harder
question — *do you think this is an app that wins? Because I don't.*

Both were right, and the first explains part of the second.

I had fixed the camera days earlier so the horizon fell inside the frame, and never
looked at what that exposed. The ground is a near-black plane with nothing on it, so the
towers ran down into a brown haze and stopped. The skyline read as pasted onto a dark
background rather than as standing anywhere — and that is the first thing anyone sees,
several seconds before a word of the interface is read.

A night city from above is mostly one thing: **dark blocks with lit lines between them.**
There are streets now — an additive grid over the ground, avenues brighter and wider than
the side streets, irregular because evenly spaced blocks read as graph paper. It is a
separate mesh rather than an emissive map, because the ground's emissive channel belongs
to the time of day: `daylight` drives it and `ground-tint` blends from the authored
colour (AC-12), and a map there would have put the streets under two owners.

Three passes to get it right, each failing in a way I should have predicted:

- **4000-unit plane, tiled 6×.** A grid that runs to the far plane converges, at grazing
  angles, into a single bright band straight across the skyline. Mipmaps and anisotropy
  soften that and cannot remove it, because the geometry really is converging.
- **1800-unit plane.** The band became the plane's own rim: additive blending draws a
  hard edge as a bright line, which is worse than what it replaced.
- **Falloff painted into the texture** — which is also why `repeat` is 1 and the block
  spacing is stated in world units. First radius fell off by the middle of the texture
  and the streets nearly vanished.

The streets go out with the windows and the lamps, because lit roads at noon is the same
defect as lamps at noon written in a third place.

### On the question

The engineering is strong and the first impression was not, and only one of those is
what a judge sees in the first three seconds. I had been scoring the product against a
rubric and the owner was scoring it against *looking at it*, which is the more honest
test and the one I kept deferring. Every real visual defect in this project has been
found the same way: by someone looking at a frame, not by reading the code that made it.

---

'''

entry = '''## 13 Sep — The model designed a hot air balloon, and it took 75 seconds

The credit came back, so the one capability that had never run live finally could: the
model writing a rig for something nobody wrote by hand.

**"un globo aerostático sobrevolando la plaza"** — fourteen parts. An envelope, a crown,
a skirt, two painted bands, a basket, and a burner flame flickering on two frequencies:

```js
let dx = Math.sin(t*0.23)*9 + Math.sin(t*0.071)*4.5;   // drift
let tilt = Math.sin(t*0.62+1.2)*0.05;                   // the envelope leaning into it
let fl = Math.sin(t*11.0)*0.22 + Math.sin(t*17.3)*0.14; // the flame
```

L3 judged it in Spanish, because the request was in Spanish, and approved it. The
screenshot is a red balloon with a white zigzag band hanging between two skyscrapers.

That is the answer to *"entonces la magia no existe realmente"*, and it cost 75 seconds,
against a 40-second budget. So the rest of the session was spent on that, and it turned
into three separate lessons.

### Effort is not the lever, and reaching for it costs the thing that matters

Same request at each setting: **high 58 s / 14 parts, medium 35 s / 13, low 16 s / 10.**
Low is the obvious fix and it is the wrong one — its balloon is a plain sphere with a
basket. The extra effort does not buy a better-*conceived* figure, it buys painted bands,
and painted bands are exactly what this path exists to be good at. Trading them for
seconds is paying in the only currency the feature has.

### The author did not need to be second

The two model calls do not depend on each other. One decides which catalogue primitives
to compose; the other designs a rig. They ran in sequence for no reason other than that
I wrote them in that order, which put both on the critical path.

They run together now, and the speculation is free to make: the offline keyword resolver
runs locally in microseconds and already knows whether the catalogue will leave something
unsaid. If it will not, the author is never started and no call is wasted. **The
deterministic floor, used as a predictor for the expensive path.** 75 s became 45 s.

### And 45 s was still the wrong number, because I was measuring the wrong window

R-8 says **"≤ 40 s from utterance to injection"**. L3 runs *after* injection — it is
advisory and never blocks, which is the whole of D-1. I had been charging an advisory
model call to a budget written for the moment the world changes.

By the time the critic speaks, the balloon has been drifting for five seconds.

Both are reported now. Utterance to injection, which is what the constraint names and
what AC-18 asserts; and the whole cycle, which is what the log prints, because someone
watching the trace finish is waiting for the total.

```
  un globo aerostático…   injected 36.6s   cycle 42.2s
  una noche de tormenta   injected 10.5s   cycle 16.2s
  make it rain            injected  8.9s   cycle 13.2s
```

The first measurement I tried put injection at 0.1 s, because the cycle's own clock
starts *after* the resolver has answered. Three different windows, and only one of them
is the one the constraint is about.

---

'''

Three complaints in one message, and the third was the one I would never have found.

### "Se queda toda la escena solo en el avión"

The camera locked on to a rig the moment one existed and never let go. Ask for an
aeroplane and the city was gone — permanently, with no way back to it.

That is not a camera decision, it is a camera *bug*: **framing something is an act with a
beginning and an end**, and this one had no end. The wide shot is the default now and
focus is a state you enter and leave. A new rig takes the frame for seven seconds because
the thing you just asked for is worth looking at, then gives it back. Tab cycles the rigs
by hand, Escape returns to the whole city.

### "No hay físicas"

`debris` is the first primitive whose correctness is a *law* rather than a preference.
Everything else is judged against what someone decided it should do — rain falls at the
speed the catalogue named. This one integrates: gravity, velocity, restitution, and a
ground that takes energy out of every bounce.

Which gives L2 something no other primitive can offer. **Total mechanical energy falls
monotonically**, because a semi-implicit integrator with restitution below one is
dissipative. That invariant is invisible in a screenshot: a world that *gains* energy
every bounce does not look broken, it looks livelier, right up until the bodies leave the
frame. It is exactly the failure WorldCoder-Bench reports as dominant — hidden state
drifting out of agreement with a scene that still looks plausible.

Verified against the bug it exists to catch, not assumed. Switching to explicit Euler —
reading velocity before the acceleration is applied rather than after, the classic
mistake — renders beautifully and fails by name:

```
energy rose on 39 frames, worst by 13.343: expected 39 to be +0
```

ground at a hard edge with no contact darkening, and no tower darkened its neighbour. An
eye reads a missing shadow before it reads anything else, and no amount of grading covers
for it. I had spent days on bloom thresholds and fog ranges without once asking why the
city had no shadows.

not a decision anybody made, it is what you get when a city is a single `InstancedMesh`
and nothing says otherwise. Real blocks are concrete beside glass beside brick, and the
difference between them is most of what stops a skyline reading as one extruded object.

from its own shaft is two buildings stacked.

a ratio of a little over two to one. That is why the city looked flat — and it is why the
shadows I had just switched on could not be seen, because *a shadow is the absence of the
key*, and if the key is only twice the fill there is nowhere for it to darken to.

eleven to one, and the faces separated immediately.

questioned the lighting model underneath it.** Bloom, vignette, grain, tone curve, a
facade texture, streets — every one of those is a layer applied *to* a render, and the
render itself had no shadows, no material variety and a fill light half as bright as its

took looking rather than reasoning: without it the facades acne, because a surface at a
grazing angle to the light samples its own depth, and under a low moon almost every face
in a city of flat slabs is at a grazing angle.

120 fps with the shadow pass in, which was the thing I expected to have to fight and did
not: the city is one instanced draw, so shadowing it is one more.

directional shapes wherever the subject has a direction, which is almost always.

    capsule    a limb, a fuselage, a torso, a branch

    cone       a NOSE, a spire, a beak, a rocket, a pine tree, a funnel
    wedge      a WING, a roof, a fin, a ramp, a blade, a sail
    pyramid    a crown, a tent, a spike, a turret cap
    torus      a wheel, a ring, a lifebuoy, a halo

render: lay out a city, and make a part the size it says it is

Five complaints in one message, and two root causes under all of them.

THE BUILDINGS WERE NEVER PLACED. They were scattered through an annulus
at random angles with random rotations, which is not a city — it is
boxes thrown at a disc. That single fact caused four of the five: there
were no streets because there were no gaps for streets to be; nothing
was well placed because nothing was placed; a rig dropped into the world
landed inside a tower; and trees had nowhere to stand.

So there is a street plan, and everything reads from it. Avenues at
irregular spacing — even spacing is graph paper, a real plan has long
avenues and short cross streets. Blocks are what is left between them.
Buildings sit inside blocks, inset from the kerb, two to a block where a
block is large enough, and square to the street: a random rotation is
the other half of why the old city read as scattered, because buildings
meet an avenue along their face, always.

The street texture is drawn from the same `AVENUES` array, which is what
makes these streets rather than a pattern — the previous grid was an
independent set of lines at an unrelated spacing laid over buildings
that were scattered, so it crossed through towers and stopped in the
middle of blocks. Asphalt lit at the kerbs rather than down the middle,
because a road brightest along its centreline reads as a strip light.
Dashed lane markings, which are small and are most of what makes a grey
band read as a road.

Tall in the middle and low at the edges, because that is what a downtown
is and it gives the skyline a shape. The open core is 260 units — wider
than the camera's 165 orbit, which the first version was not: the camera
ended up inside the city looking down an avenue with two towers filling
the frame.

Trees along the avenues, skipped near the plaza. They carry the only
green in a scene that is otherwise blue sky, sodium orange and
near-black stone, and one colour that belongs to nothing else is what
stops a palette reading as a filter.

Rooftop clutter — tanks, stair houses, plant. What separates a skyline
that was built from one that was extruded is what sits on top of it.

AND A PART WAS NOT THE SIZE IT SAID IT WAS. The radius of a capsule,
cylinder or cone was `max(x, z)`, so a torso authored [2.6, 3.4, 1.7]
became a sausage of radius 2.6 — and at that radius it swallowed its own
arms, which the pose had placed 5.5 units off the centre line, inside a
shape the renderer had decided was 5.2 units fat. "Person walking a dog"
rendered as one featureless blob.

Every shape is now built at unit radius and scaled by its declared
extents, so `size` means in the renderer what the prompt promises it
means: half-extents in x, y, z. A part that says it is thin is thin, and

Four faults, one visible symptom: a person standing in a milky void,

to twelve parts, so the dog was writing its legs into the person's. Both
rigs rendered — as a legless figure over a pile of loose sticks, with
every index in state pointing at a real part, just the wrong one. Two
tests now hold the class shut for every rig: a pose may not address a
part the rig does not have, and a rig may not declare a part its pose
never places.

Scale was the second. The city is metric — a street tree's trunk is 9
units, a road is 11 across — and rigs are authored at "about 40 units
tall" because that is the only scale a model can hold in its head
alongside a thousand-unit city. FIGURE_SCALE converts once, on the rig's
root transform, so rigs keep authoring in the units the prompt promises
and a pedestrian comes out 1.8 units tall.

That made the camera wrong in turn. It orbited the world origin, which
is right when the city is the subject and absurd at a four-unit dolly,
and it handed focus back after seven seconds — which broke the product
(the thing you just asked for is not a passing event) and the
measurement with it, since L3 then photographed the skyline and reported
no person and no dog.

The rigs themselves are rebuilt on forward kinematics. Setting a part's
position and its rotation independently is a contradiction: rotating a
segment about its centre moves both ends, so the elbow the upper arm
reaches is not the elbow the forearm was placed at, and the gaps opened
and closed through the stride. A joint is now computed once and the next
segment hung off it. Both components of that offset take a minus; the
natural thing to type — minus for the downward term, plus for the
forward one — hinges the joint sideways.

The person gains a chest and waist instead of one capsule, feet, and a
leash that comes out of the hand chain, which is what makes the pair
read as someone walking a dog rather than a figure near an animal.

The near ground is paved in the shader. The street map is drawn once
across 2,460 units — under one texel per metre — so at pedestrian range
it renders as an untextured plane, and a figure standing on a void reads
as a figure that was never placed in the world. 2.4-unit slabs with cell
noise have no resolution to run out of; they mix in by camera distance,
because past eighty units they would alias and the drawn map is the
right answer anyway.

L3 kept reporting "there is no human figure" about frames with a person
in them, and the cause was ordering, not eyesight: the camera was
pointed at the new rig from the `accept` step, and L3 judges a candidate
*before* it is accepted. The one layer that looks at pictures was
photographing the skyline it was about to leave, on every figure
utterance ever run.

The camera now follows the world's published state — a subject in state
is a subject to frame — which is the rule the framing code above it
already stated and needs no cooperation from the cascade. A candidate
mounted for review is in state, so it is framed, so it is what gets
judged. The critic's verdict on "a person walking a dog" went from "no
human figure and no dog" to "the rear-view person with a small dog
beside them reads clearly".

The shot also publishes its own arrival ramp under `mix`, the convention
every primitive that takes time already uses, so `settle()` waits for
the move to land without a special case for cameras.

The rest is scale. Making figures metric left the bounds and the older
rigs behind: MAX_SIZE was 40 authored units, which is 1.8 metres, so a
bus could not be built and a rig could not reach higher than 18 metres —
a hard ceiling on anything that flies. They are restated in the metres
they now mean, and exported, because both tests asserting them had
copied the numbers and so stopped testing them the moment they moved.

The car was a briefcase on an eleven-metre road and the tree was a tenth
the height of the street trees the city already plants; both are rebuilt
at the canon. The authoring prompt gains the world's scale table in the
model's own units, including the one it gets wrong: a plane authored at
y = 300 sounds high and is parked on the road, against a skyline of
6,600.

cd /Users/ricardo/verbo; git add -A; git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
Give each rig its own ground, and a walk without a cusp in it

Two faults, one complaint: the figures walked into each other and did
not walk like anything.

Every figure in the catalogue was authored with the same origin, because
each was written and looked at on its own. Ask for a person and then for
a car and both are mounted on the same three square metres, pacing the
same short line through each other. Nothing in state is wrong, which is
why no oracle caught it and why it needed a test instead.

A station is now claimed by name and kept — the same name is the same
rig being replaced, so re-running an utterance puts it back rather than
walking it across the plaza, and a different name gets its own ground.
The layout is a phyllotaxis spiral: no two stations line up, spacing
stays even however many are claimed, and headings fall out of it, so the
figures do not all pace one axis like a parade. The test measures how
far each rig actually strays from its station over a full cycle of its
own animation and requires the stations to be further apart than the sum
of those reaches — a longer stride fails there rather than on screen.

The walk itself paced a straight segment and reversed by setting
`facing` from 0 to pi between one frame and the next: a person spinning
180 degrees instantly, with the dog teleporting to their other side. No
smoothing fixes that, because the path has a cusp — a body walking a
line has to stop to turn, and a rig cannot stop. An oval has no cusp.
Heading is the direction of travel, so it is defined and continuous at
every instant, and the turn happens because the walker is walking a
curve, which is what someone pacing a plaza does.

Every part is now placed in the walker's own frame and turned into the
world once, which is also what let the dog keep to their left instead of
choosing a side from a boolean that flipped twice a lap.

Escape lost its guard. It was the documented way back to the wide shot
and it was unreachable: the prompt holds focus after every utterance, so
the one key that leaves a close shot never fired for anyone who had just
said something.
MSG

Have CI verify what a GPU-less runner can honestly verify

Two runs, two ways of failing, one cause: a GitHub runner has no GPU.
Its WebGPU is SwiftShader, which comes up and then drops the device
mid-run — twenty-four "Instance dropped in popErrorScope" errors, after
which every frame capture waits on a device that is gone, and eighteen
of twenty-six browser tests time out. Forcing the WebGL2 path instead
does render: the fallback test passed in run one, in 27.5 seconds. Put
the whole suite on it and every test sits on the wrong side of the
thirty-second timeout, which is how the second attempt turned eighteen
failures into twenty-three.

Either way CI would be measuring a software rasteriser rather than the
product, and the way to make it green — loosen the timeouts until a
rasteriser passes — would be the exact failure this project exists to

of twenty-six browser tests time out. Forcing the WebGL2 path instead
does render: the fallback test passed in run one, in 27.5 seconds. Put
the whole suite on it and every test sits on the wrong side of the
thirty-second timeout, which is how the second attempt turned eighteen
failures into twenty-three.

product, and the way to make it green — loosen the timeouts until a
rasteriser passes — would be the exact failure this project exists to
argue against.

Let a visitor's own key reach all three model-backed components

Only the resolver had a browser path. On the published site — static, no
proxy — a visitor who pasted a key got Claude resolving their sentences
and then a 405 from /api/critique on every verb, so L3 never judged a
single frame where anyone could see it, and /api/figure was unreachable
too, so any request needing a rig the catalogue does not have quietly
fell back to keywords.

Three quarters of what this project argues was demonstrable only on a
machine running a server, which is the one place it needs no
demonstrating.

The critic and the rig author now follow the order the resolver already
used: proxy first, the visitor's key second. Same classes, same prompts,
same schemas — only the transport differs, which is what makes a hosted
visitor's run evidence of the same system rather than of a demo.

Verified against a production build with a key: "make it cozy and
cinematic" came back judged — "the warm gradient sky, volumetric light
shaft, haze and rain streaks over a receding boulevard carry the cozy
cinematic mood" — and "un astronauta caminando por la plaza", which no
catalogue entry covers, was authored, injected and judged as "the white
suited humanoid mid-stride on an open paved plaza".
